input.reason: Prediction called for ≥0.70 accuracy on fresh unassisted material; the Quest delivered 3/3 unseen, unassisted, independent-probe correct readings across equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation (accuracy 1.0), and the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization error never appeared. That supports transfer at the evidence limit of independent performance — it does not establish synthesis, since every Quest item still isolated one target at a time. Boss eligibility is met on fresh unassisted evidence, so the next instrument must force the three targets to collide inside one problem. The one loud counter-signal is engagement: both runs finalized at fun 1/5 with confusion and hesitation flagged and no replay requested, while accuracy stayed perfect. Correct answers plus no enjoyment reads as an instrument that was too thin and too talky for a 9-year-old who is clearly not being challenged, so the Boss escalates real difficulty and gives him something concrete to move and something real to lose.
preserve: Unseen material only, unassisted, no scaffold hints before an answer is committed
All three targets kept live: equal-groups construction, missing-factor recovery, word-problem interpretation with distractor quantities
Short total runtime near two to three minutes; no long reading blocks
change: Stop asking one target per question — require two or three targets resolved inside a single committed action
Replace text-answer prompts with direct physical manipulation the child drags and locks
Raise difficulty sharply: unknown group size, deliberately unusable leftover quantities, and a hard limit on attempts
Give the run a visible cost for being wrong so success feels earned
testNext: Can he build equal groups when the group size is the unknown rather than the total?
Does he reject distractor quantities that cannot form equal groups instead of forcing them in?
Does synthesis hold when the missing factor must be recovered before the word problem can even be read correctly?
Does a hands-on, high-consequence format move engagement off 1/5 while accuracy stays high?

input.nextTitle: Six Crates, One Rope, No Second Try
input.nextAcademicTarget: math.multiplication.synthesis — construct equal groups with an unknown group size, recover a missing factor, and interpret a word-problem constraint containing distractor quantities, all resolved within one committed action on unseen material
input.nextMechanic: A weight-balanced cargo rope where the child drags supply crates into a fixed number of sling loops; the rope only holds if every loop carries an identical load, and leftover crates must be left behind on purpose.
input.nextTheme: A supply rope strung across a flooded canyon at dusk. A field camp on the far side is waiting. The rope is fraying and it will bear exactly one crossing.
input.nextOpeningPurpose: Open on the rope already creaking with the camp's radio voice giving one line: "Loops must match or the rope snaps." No tutorial, no warm-up question — the first thing the child does is touch a crate.
input.nextCreatorPrompt: Build a three-stage rope-crossing for a 9-year-old who is bored by being asked easy questions and needs to be treated as capable. The screen shows a fraying rope with a fixed number of empty sling loops and a dock pile of numbered supply crates. The child drags crates into loops, then pulls a lever to send the rope. The rope only survives if every loop holds exactly the same total. Stage one: the radio says the camp needs 24 ration units delivered across 6 loops — the crate values are given but the per-loop amount is not, so he must recover the group size himself. Stage two: the loop count is hidden and only stated inside a spoken supply order that also mentions two quantities that are irrelevant (the canyon depth and the number of days the camp has been waiting), so he must read the order, discard the noise, and deduce how many loops to fill. Stage three: the dock pile deliberately contains more crates than can be evenly divided — he must load the correct equal grouping and leave the surplus crates on the dock, and the rope snaps if he crams them in "to be safe." Every mis-send costs a strand of the rope, visible and audible. Keep spoken text to one or two short lines per stage. The payoff at the end should be the camp lights coming on across the canyon, not a badge or a cheer. Do not restate the multiplication as an equation for him at any point before he commits — if you show the arithmetic, the evidence is gone.
input.nextStakesDesign: The rope has three strands and one crossing. Every incorrect send tears a strand with a visible snap and the crates in that loop fall into the water and are gone from the dock pile for the rest of the run — so a wrong answer makes the remaining stages genuinely harder, not just retried. Lose all three strands and the rope drops: the run ends with the camp lights staying dark across the canyon and the child has to start the crossing over from the dock. What is at risk is the delivery he has been building for two minutes and the supplies he was trusted with.
input.nextFailureMode: Three failure paths, all real. Forcing surplus crates into loops to avoid leaving anything behind overloads the rope and snaps a strand immediately. Treating a distractor quantity in the spoken order as the loop count produces unequal loads and a snap. Guessing a familiar factor pair instead of deriving the unknown group size loads the loops unevenly and snaps. Three snaps and the crossing fails outright — dark camp, restart from the dock, crates lost. He can be beaten by this, and that is the point: he has answered everything correctly twice and rated both runs 1 out of 5.
input.nextEscalation: Stage one gives him the total and the loop count and hides only the group size — one target, tight and fast, to teach the rope's rule by using it. Stage two hides the loop count inside spoken language padded with two irrelevant numbers, so interpretation and missing-factor recovery must happen together before a single crate moves. Stage three removes the guarantee that everything fits: the dock is overstocked, the correct answer requires deliberately abandoning supplies, and the rope is already down at least one strand if he stumbled earlier. Time pressure rises only through the rope's creak growing louder, never a countdown.
input.nextMechanicSpec: Finger or cursor drags a numbered crate from the dock pile into one of the sling loops hanging on the rope; the crate snaps into the loop and the loop's running total appears on its tag as a number that updates live. Loops sag lower as they get heavier, so uneven loading is visible as a lopsided rope before he commits. A long-press on a loaded crate returns it to the dock. Pulling the launch lever commits the send: if all loops match the required equal load, the rope glides level across the canyon and the crates land at the camp. If any loop differs, the rope jerks, one strand visibly frays and snaps with a crack, the overloaded loop tips and its crates tumble into the water and disappear from the dock pile permanently, and the remaining strand count drops on screen. On the third snap the whole rope falls, the far bank goes dark, and the dock resets with the run marked failed.
input.nextMathematicalHook: Equal groups turn a rope into a scale: it is not the total weight that breaks the rope, it is the imbalance. A child discovers that 24 units across 6 loops crosses safely while 24 units piled 10-6-4-2-1-1 tears the rope apart — same total, opposite outcome. And the strangest part is that winning sometimes means leaving good crates behind, because 26 units simply cannot be shared into 6 equal loops no matter how badly the camp needs them.
input.revisedHypothesis: Lab Learner transfers single-target multiplication reasoning to fresh material with high accuracy; it remains untested whether he can synthesize equal-groups construction, missing-factor recovery with an unknown group size, and distractor-laden word-problem interpretation inside one committed action, and whether a manipulative, high-consequence format raises engagement above the 1/5 he has reported twice while accuracy holds.
